questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: A gram-negative rod from a urine culture is streaked onto eosin methylene blue (EMB) agar and produces the colonies shown. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: On EMB agar, lactose fermenters generally stain black, but E. coli is the exception: it forms colonies with a distinctive green metallic sheen. Klebsiella also ferments lactose but lacks the sheen; Proteus, Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose fermenters.
explanation.whyCorrect: On EMB agar, lactose fermenters generally stain black, but E. coli is the exception: it forms colonies with a distinctive green metallic sheen. Klebsiella also ferments lactose but lacks the sheen; Proteus, Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose fermenters.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: A gram-negative enteric rod grown on blood agar shows clearing of the agar around its colonies, as shown. Among the major Enterobacteriaceae, which organism characteristically produces this hemolytic pattern?

explanation.summary: The image shows beta hemolysis (complete clearing of red cells around the colonies). Among the Enterobacteriaceae covered, only E. coli is beta-hemolytic, although hemolysis is not normally used to tell family members apart.
explanation.whyCorrect: The image shows beta hemolysis (complete clearing of red cells around the colonies). Among the Enterobacteriaceae covered, only E. coli is beta-hemolytic, although hemolysis is not normally used to tell family members apart.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: A non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod is inoculated into triple sugar iron (TSI) agar, giving the result shown (red slant, black butt). Which pair of Enterobacteriaceae characteristically produces this black precipitate?

explanation.summary: The black precipitate is ferrous sulfide, formed when H2S reacts with the ferrous ions in TSI agar. Salmonella, Proteus and Citrobacter produce H2S; E. coli and K. pneumoniae do not, and Shigella is H2S negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: The black precipitate is ferrous sulfide, formed when H2S reacts with the ferrous ions in TSI agar. Salmonella, Proteus and Citrobacter produce H2S; E. coli and K. pneumoniae do not, and Shigella is H2S negative.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: The molecule shown is found in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli. What is the clinical use of its variable, repeating outermost (leftmost) segment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anchoring the molecule in the inner (cytoplasmic) membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Serotyping E. coli strains to track outbreaks

explanation.summary: This is lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that can drive inflammation and sepsis. Its O-specific polysaccharide (O antigen) varies from strain to strain. Together with the flagellar H antigen, it is used to serotype strains such as O157:H7 and trace outbreaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is lipopolysaccharide (LPS), an endotoxin that can drive inflammation and sepsis. Its O-specific polysaccharide (O antigen) varies from strain to strain. Together with the flagellar H antigen, it is used to serotype strains such as O157:H7 and trace outbreaks.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: An infant in a developing country has noninflammatory watery diarrhea. Electron micrographs of the small-bowel brush border show bacteria sitting on raised actin pedestals with loss of the surrounding microvilli, as shown. Which E. coli pathotype is responsible?

explanation.summary: EPEC attaches to the small-intestinal brush border and causes attaching-and-effacing lesions: microvilli are lost and actin pedestals form. This disrupts absorption and causes watery, noninflammatory diarrhea, mostly in infants in developing countries. ETEC acts through enterotoxins, and EIEC invades the colon.
explanation.whyCorrect: EPEC attaches to the small-intestinal brush border and causes attaching-and-effacing lesions: microvilli are lost and actin pedestals form. This disrupts absorption and causes watery, noninflammatory diarrhea, mostly in infants in developing countries. ETEC acts through enterotoxins, and EIEC invades the colon.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 1 of 2)
questions.stem: The toxin released by the organism shown can enter the circulation and damage glomerular endothelial cells. Which clinical triad results?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status

explanation.summary: EHEC (e.g., O157:H7) releases Shiga toxin. Damage to the glomerular endothelium causes platelet aggregation and microthrombi that fragment red cells. The result is hemolytic uremic syndrome: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: EHEC (e.g., O157:H7) releases Shiga toxin. Damage to the glomerular endothelium causes platelet aggregation and microthrombi that fragment red cells. The result is hemolytic uremic syndrome: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney failure.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: A man with alcohol use disorder develops fever and a cough productive of thick, blood-tinged sputum after an episode of vomiting. Serial chest x-rays show a dense right upper lobe consolidation that progresses to a large cavity (arrows). Sputum grows a lactose-fermenting, nonmotile, indole-negative gram-negative rod. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: K. pneumoniae causes pneumonia in people with alcohol use disorder, who are prone to aspiration, and in hospitalized patients. Severe cases become necrotizing and form cavities. The large mucoid capsule produces the classic thick, bloody 'red currant jelly' sputum.
explanation.whyCorrect: K. pneumoniae causes pneumonia in people with alcohol use disorder, who are prone to aspiration, and in hospitalized patients. Severe cases become necrotizing and form cavities. The large mucoid capsule produces the classic thick, bloody 'red currant jelly' sputum.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: Two lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods are each tested with the assay shown. The left tube is negative and the right tube shows a red layer after reagent is added. Which organism most likely gave the right-hand result?

explanation.summary: This is the indole test: a red color after reagent is added means the organism produced indole from tryptophan. E. coli is indole positive. K. pneumoniae, Enterobacter and P. mirabilis are indole negative, which helps separate E. coli from the other lactose fermenters.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the indole test: a red color after reagent is added means the organism produced indole from tryptophan. E. coli is indole positive. K. pneumoniae, Enterobacter and P. mirabilis are indole negative, which helps separate E. coli from the other lactose fermenters.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: A sputum culture on MacConkey agar grows the pink, very slimy colonies shown. The organism is a nonmotile, indole-negative gram-negative rod. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: The pink color means lactose fermentation. The thick, slimy look comes from the large mucoid capsule of K. pneumoniae. Being nonmotile and indole negative separates it from E. coli, and Proteus, Salmonella and Shigella do not ferment lactose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pink color means lactose fermentation. The thick, slimy look comes from the large mucoid capsule of K. pneumoniae. Being nonmotile and indole negative separates it from E. coli, and Proteus, Salmonella and Shigella do not ferment lactose.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: A urine isolate grows the pink, dry, non-mucoid colonies shown on MacConkey agar. The organism is motile and indole positive. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Pink colonies on MacConkey mean a fast lactose fermenter. Motility, a positive indole test and the absence of the slimy mucoid capsule point to E. coli rather than K. pneumoniae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pink colonies on MacConkey mean a fast lactose fermenter. Motility, a positive indole test and the absence of the slimy mucoid capsule point to E. coli rather than K. pneumoniae.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: During a urinary tract infection, an organism uses the enzyme reaction shown, which raises urine pH. Which type of kidney stone is most strongly linked to this process?

explanation.summary: Urease splits urea into ammonia and CO2, making the urine alkaline. Calcium-containing compounds then precipitate, and the ammonia forms struvite, which can grow into large staghorn calculi. Proteus mirabilis is the classic urease producer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Urease splits urea into ammonia and CO2, making the urine alkaline. Calcium-containing compounds then precipitate, and the ammonia forms struvite, which can grow into large staghorn calculi. Proteus mirabilis is the classic urease producer.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: A woman with recurrent urinary tract infections has an abdominal x-ray showing large branching radiopaque calculi filling the left renal collecting system, as shown. Her urine is alkaline and grows a swarming, non-lactose-fermenting, urease-positive gram-negative rod. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: The x-ray shows staghorn calculi. P. mirabilis produces urease, which alkalinizes the urine and leads to struvite stones that can branch like deer antlers. Its swarming motility and lack of lactose fermentation identify it in the lab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The x-ray shows staghorn calculi. P. mirabilis produces urease, which alkalinizes the urine and leads to struvite stones that can branch like deer antlers. Its swarming motility and lack of lactose fermentation identify it in the lab.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: The branched stone shown was surgically removed from a renal pelvis in a patient with recurrent UTIs. What is the most likely composition of this stone?

explanation.summary: This is a staghorn calculus, a branching stone shaped like deer horns. Staghorn calculi are struvite stones that form when urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis alkalinize the urine and generate ammonia. They can get so large that surgery is needed to remove them.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a staghorn calculus, a branching stone shaped like deer horns. Staghorn calculi are struvite stones that form when urease-producing bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis alkalinize the urine and generate ammonia. They can get so large that surgery is needed to remove them.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: A gram-negative rod from a hospitalized, immunocompromised patient is a slow lactose fermenter, motile and urease negative, and its colonies have the color shown. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Some Serratia species produce a red pigment (prodigiosin), which distinguishes Serratia from Citrobacter, the other slow lactose fermenter. Not all Serratia strains are pigmented. Serratia mainly causes opportunistic infections in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some Serratia species produce a red pigment (prodigiosin), which distinguishes Serratia from Citrobacter, the other slow lactose fermenter. Not all Serratia strains are pigmented. Serratia mainly causes opportunistic infections in hospitalized or immunocompromised patients.

questions.topicName: Enterobacteriaceae (Part 2 of 2)
questions.stem: The pinkish-orange discoloration along the grout of the bathroom tiles shown is a biofilm. Its pigment reveals which environmental gram-negative rod?

explanation.summary: Serratia is widespread in soil and water. Pigment-producing strains make a red pigment, which shows when a biofilm, such as the pink film on shower grout, contains Serratia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serratia is widespread in soil and water. Pigment-producing strains make a red pigment, which shows when a biofilm, such as the pink film on shower grout, contains Serratia.

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter all use the needle-like structure shown, which spans the inner and outer membranes of the gram-negative cell envelope. What is its function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pumping antibiotics out of the bacterial cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Injecting bacterial effector proteins directly into host cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Propelling the bacterium through the intestinal mucus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transferring plasmid DNA to another bacterium by conjugation

explanation.summary: This is a type III secretion system (T3SS). Its needle injects effector proteins into host cells, which promotes bacterial entry (for example through M cells) and intracellular survival. Motility comes from flagella, and DNA transfer happens through conjugation.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is a type III secretion system (T3SS). Its needle injects effector proteins into host cells, which promotes bacterial entry (for example through M cells) and intracellular survival. Motility comes from flagella, and DNA transfer happens through conjugation.

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: The small, scarred spleen shown, with multiple dark infarcts, came from a patient with sickle cell anemia. Loss of splenic function puts this patient at increased risk of disseminated infection, including osteomyelitis, from which enteric pathogen?

explanation.summary: Recurrent splenic infarction in sickle cell disease leads to functional asplenia. Patients without a working spleen are at higher risk of disseminated salmonellosis, with rare complications such as septicemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis and meningitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent splenic infarction in sickle cell disease leads to functional asplenia. Patients without a working spleen are at higher risk of disseminated salmonellosis, with rare complications such as septicemia, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis and meningitis.

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: A traveler returning from South Asia has had a week of fever, headache, malaise, constipation and hepatosplenomegaly. He has the transient maculopapular truncal rash shown. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Typhoid fever, caused by S. Typhi (and S. Paratyphi), presents with fever, constitutional symptoms, constipation or diarrhea, and possible bacteremia with hepatosplenomegaly. A transient maculopapular rash on the trunk is distinctive and does not occur in nontyphoidal salmonellosis. S. Typhi has only human reservoirs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typhoid fever, caused by S. Typhi (and S. Paratyphi), presents with fever, constitutional symptoms, constipation or diarrhea, and possible bacteremia with hepatosplenomegaly. A transient maculopapular rash on the trunk is distinctive and does not occur in nontyphoidal salmonellosis. S. Typhi has only human reservoirs.

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: A stool isolate from a patient who ate undercooked chicken is grown on the bottom half of the MacConkey plate shown, beside a pink lactose fermenter on the top half. The isolate is motile and produces H2S. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: The bottom colonies are colorless, so the organism does not ferment lactose. A motile, H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter linked to poultry is Salmonella. Shigella is nonmotile and H2S negative, and E. coli and Klebsiella ferment lactose (pink).
explanation.whyCorrect: The bottom colonies are colorless, so the organism does not ferment lactose. A motile, H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter linked to poultry is Salmonella. Shigella is nonmotile and H2S negative, and E. coli and Klebsiella ferment lactose (pink).

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: A motile, oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod from a patient with bloody diarrhea gives the triple sugar iron (TSI) result shown: red slant, yellow butt and a black precipitate. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: The yellow butt shows glucose fermentation (acid), and the black precipitate shows H2S production. Salmonella ferments glucose, makes H2S and is motile. Shigella shows no black precipitate and is nonmotile, which separates the two.
explanation.whyCorrect: The yellow butt shows glucose fermentation (acid), and the black precipitate shows H2S production. Salmonella ferments glucose, makes H2S and is motile. Shigella shows no black precipitate and is nonmotile, which separates the two.

questions.topicName: Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter spp.
questions.stem: A patient has fever, abdominal cramping and diarrhea a few days after eating undercooked poultry. A stool Gram stain shows the organisms seen here. Two weeks later she develops ascending leg weakness. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: The stain shows gram-negative curved, comma- or S-shaped rods. That shape separates Campylobacter from Salmonella and Shigella, which are straight rods. C. jejuni is the most common cause of bacterial diarrhea in the U.S. and the most common cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stain shows gram-negative curved, comma- or S-shaped rods. That shape separates Campylobacter from Salmonella and Shigella, which are straight rods. C. jejuni is the most common cause of bacterial diarrhea in the U.S. and the most common cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A patient develops the severe eye infection shown after using artificial tears from a product later recalled for bacterial contamination. Green pus is present. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Severe keratitis with green pus after contaminated eye drops points to P. aeruginosa; the green color reflects its pigment production. A 2023 artificial-tear recall involved an extensively drug-resistant Pseudomonas strain that caused vision loss and deaths.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe keratitis with green pus after contaminated eye drops points to P. aeruginosa; the green color reflects its pigment production. A 2023 artificial-tear recall involved an extensively drug-resistant Pseudomonas strain that caused vision loss and deaths.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: The electron micrograph shows a gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacillus with a single polar flagellum, isolated from a hospitalized patient. Which organism best fits this appearance?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas spp. are gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli that are motile by a single polar flagellum. Acinetobacter, by contrast, is a non-motile coccobacillus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas spp. are gram-negative, non-spore-forming bacilli that are motile by a single polar flagellum. Acinetobacter, by contrast, is a non-motile coccobacillus.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: These blue-green colonies grew from a burn wound of a hospitalized patient. Which pigment produced by this organism is blue and toxic to leukocytes and epithelial cells?

explanation.summary: P. aeruginosa makes two pigments that give its colonies a blue-to-aqua color. Pyocyanin is the blue pigment that is toxic to cells, including leukocytes. Pyoverdine is the yellow, fluorescent, iron-binding pigment.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. aeruginosa makes two pigments that give its colonies a blue-to-aqua color. Pyocyanin is the blue pigment that is toxic to cells, including leukocytes. Pyoverdine is the yellow, fluorescent, iron-binding pigment.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A broth culture of a gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacillus glows yellow-green under UV light, as shown. Which bacterial product causes this fluorescence?

explanation.summary: Pyoverdine is a yellow, fluorescent pigment of P. aeruginosa that binds iron. It makes Pseudomonas cultures and infected tissue fluoresce under UV light. Pyocyanin is the blue, cell-toxic pigment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyoverdine is a yellow, fluorescent pigment of P. aeruginosa that binds iron. It makes Pseudomonas cultures and infected tissue fluoresce under UV light. Pyocyanin is the blue, cell-toxic pigment.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A healthy adult develops the tender, itchy red papules and pustules centered on hair follicles shown here after soaking in a poorly maintained hot tub. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Hot tub folliculitis is caused by water-loving Pseudomonas spp. that enter skin opened up by prolonged soaking. Papules and pustules cluster around hair follicles. It usually resolves on its own but can recur if the water source is not properly maintained.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hot tub folliculitis is caused by water-loving Pseudomonas spp. that enter skin opened up by prolonged soaking. Papules and pustules cluster around hair follicles. It usually resolves on its own but can recur if the water source is not properly maintained.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: An elderly patient with diabetes has severe ear pain, purulent discharge, and the destructive ear canal infection shown, along with hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hot tub folliculitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute otitis media caused by Moraxella catarrhalis

explanation.summary: In diabetic or immunocompromised patients, Pseudomonas otitis externa can invade deeper tissue and bone (malignant otitis externa). Involvement of cranial nerves IX-XII causes trouble swallowing, hoarseness, and difficulty speaking. This is a life-threatening infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: In diabetic or immunocompromised patients, Pseudomonas otitis externa can invade deeper tissue and bone (malignant otitis externa). Involvement of cranial nerves IX-XII causes trouble swallowing, hoarseness, and difficulty speaking. This is a life-threatening infection.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A patient with large third-degree burns develops spreading, darkening, necrotic skin over the injured limb, as shown, with greenish discoloration of the wound. Which organism is a classic cause of this infection?

explanation.summary: Large third-degree burns are typically infected by Pseudomonas spp., which colonize necrotic tissue and damage the host with their virulence factors. Burn-induced neutropenia raises the risk of dissemination, and septicemia is a common complication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Large third-degree burns are typically infected by Pseudomonas spp., which colonize necrotic tissue and damage the host with their virulence factors. Burn-induced neutropenia raises the risk of dissemination, and septicemia is a common complication.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A wound in a patient with severe burns glows when examined under UV light, as shown. Which organism most likely infects this wound?

explanation.summary: P. aeruginosa produces pyoverdine, a fluorescent pigment, so infected burn tissue can glow under UV light. Pseudomonas is a common cause of infection in large third-degree burns.
explanation.whyCorrect: P. aeruginosa produces pyoverdine, a fluorescent pigment, so infected burn tissue can glow under UV light. Pseudomonas is a common cause of infection in large third-degree burns.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A patient who stepped on a nail develops a deep wound with the greenish purulent drainage shown. Which organism does the green pus most suggest?

explanation.summary: Greenish purulent drainage suggests P. aeruginosa because of its pigments. Puncture injuries such as stepping on a nail can carry the organism into deep tissue and cause osteomyelitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Greenish purulent drainage suggests P. aeruginosa because of its pigments. Puncture injuries such as stepping on a nail can carry the organism into deep tissue and cause osteomyelitis.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: The ulcer shown is on the foot of a patient with diabetes. Besides S. aureus and streptococci, which gram-negative bacillus is among the most common causes of complicated infections of such ulcers?

explanation.summary: Diabetic foot infections are often polymicrobial. S. aureus and streptococci are important pathogens, and P. aeruginosa appears in more complicated infections. Mixed and antibiotic-resistant infections make treatment difficult.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diabetic foot infections are often polymicrobial. S. aureus and streptococci are important pathogens, and P. aeruginosa appears in more complicated infections. Mixed and antibiotic-resistant infections make treatment difficult.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: Poor cleaning or replacement of the item shown is a classic risk factor for a sight-threatening corneal infection by which organism?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas spp. are common in the environment and can build up in contaminated contact lens cases and solution, then infect the eye, usually after a corneal abrasion. Pseudomonas keratitis often causes permanent damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas spp. are common in the environment and can build up in contaminated contact lens cases and solution, then infect the eye, usually after a corneal abrasion. Pseudomonas keratitis often causes permanent damage.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A patient has the corneal infection shown, caused by a gram-negative, oxidase-positive bacillus. Which history most strongly predisposes to this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Soaking in a poorly maintained hot tub

choices.label: B
choices.text: Poor cleaning or replacement of contact lenses

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas keratitis usually follows corneal abrasion or other eye trauma, and contaminated contact lenses or lens solution are a classic source. These infections commonly cause permanent damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas keratitis usually follows corneal abrasion or other eye trauma, and contaminated contact lenses or lens solution are a classic source. These infections commonly cause permanent damage.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: The illustration contrasts a normal airway with the thick, sticky mucus of an autosomal recessive CFTR disease. Which organism, often as mucoid strains, is most associated with chronic lung infection and progressive lung destruction in this disease?

explanation.summary: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus lets bacteria colonize deep in the lungs. Mucoid, alginate-producing P. aeruginosa is classically linked to chronic CF lung infection, inflammation, and progressive lung destruction. Respiratory failure from chronic infection is the most common cause of death in CF.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus lets bacteria colonize deep in the lungs. Mucoid, alginate-producing P. aeruginosa is classically linked to chronic CF lung infection, inflammation, and progressive lung destruction. Respiratory failure from chronic infection is the most common cause of death in CF.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: Two strains of Pseudomonas are grown on the plate shown. The glistening, slimy strain on the right was most likely isolated from which patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A healthy hot tub user with folliculitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A child with acute otitis media

explanation.summary: Mucoid strains of P. aeruginosa make an alginate capsule that helps them adhere to and colonize mucus. They are classically isolated from the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients with chronic infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucoid strains of P. aeruginosa make an alginate capsule that helps them adhere to and colonize mucus. They are classically isolated from the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients with chronic infection.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A child with Pseudomonas bacteremia develops the dark, necrotic skin lesions on the face shown here. What is the name of these lesions?

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum is a necrotic skin lesion seen with bloodstream spread of Pseudomonas spp. It is a fairly unique presentation of Pseudomonas septicemia, although its absence does not exclude Pseudomonas infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ecthyma gangrenosum is a necrotic skin lesion seen with bloodstream spread of Pseudomonas spp. It is a fairly unique presentation of Pseudomonas septicemia, although its absence does not exclude Pseudomonas infection.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A child with septicemia has the scattered lesions shown, some with dark necrotic centers. Which organism classically causes this bloodstream-associated skin finding?

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum is classically linked to hematogenous spread of Pseudomonas spp. Most Pseudomonas infections look like those of other bacteria, but this lesion is a fairly distinctive clue to Pseudomonas septicemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ecthyma gangrenosum is classically linked to hematogenous spread of Pseudomonas spp. Most Pseudomonas infections look like those of other bacteria, but this lesion is a fairly distinctive clue to Pseudomonas septicemia.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: The lesions shown in a child with Pseudomonas septicemia began as red macules or papules. If they progress, what do they finally become?

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum starts as a red macule or papule, develops into pustules and bullae, and finally forms a necrotic ulcer. It accompanies hematogenous spread of Pseudomonas spp.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ecthyma gangrenosum starts as a red macule or papule, develops into pustules and bullae, and finally forms a necrotic ulcer. It accompanies hematogenous spread of Pseudomonas spp.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: This close-up shows a necrotic skin ulcer in a patient with Pseudomonas bacteremia. In which body areas does this lesion most commonly appear?

explanation.summary: Ecthyma gangrenosum, the necrotic lesion of Pseudomonas septicemia, can appear almost anywhere but most often involves the anogenital and axillary areas.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ecthyma gangrenosum, the necrotic lesion of Pseudomonas septicemia, can appear almost anywhere but most often involves the anogenital and axillary areas.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: An infant has a cloudy, infected left cornea and necrotic skin lesions on the face, as shown. A single disseminated infection explains both findings. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Disseminated Pseudomonas infection can cause both keratitis and ecthyma gangrenosum, the necrotic skin lesion of Pseudomonas bacteremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disseminated Pseudomonas infection can cause both keratitis and ecthyma gangrenosum, the necrotic skin lesion of Pseudomonas bacteremia.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A sputum sample from a ventilated ICU patient grows the aqua-green colonies shown. The organism is a gram-negative bacillus that does not ferment lactose and is oxidase-positive. Which organism is it?

explanation.summary: Pseudomonas spp. are gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive bacilli whose colonies are aqua or green because of pyocyanin and pyoverdine. Lactose fermentation would point to E. coli or K. pneumoniae, and an oxidase-negative result to Salmonella or Shigella. Acinetobacter colonies are colorless or creamy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomonas spp. are gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive bacilli whose colonies are aqua or green because of pyocyanin and pyoverdine. Lactose fermentation would point to E. coli or K. pneumoniae, and an oxidase-negative result to Salmonella or Shigella. Acinetobacter colonies are colorless or creamy.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: Two P. aeruginosa isolates are shown side by side. Which bacterial product gives the right-hand isolate its slimy appearance?

explanation.summary: Mucoid strains make an alginate capsule, a polysaccharide that absorbs many times its weight in water and helps the bacteria cling to and colonize mucus. These strains are classically associated with chronic cystic fibrosis lung infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucoid strains make an alginate capsule, a polysaccharide that absorbs many times its weight in water and helps the bacteria cling to and colonize mucus. These strains are classically associated with chronic cystic fibrosis lung infection.

questions.topicName: Pseudomonas species and other closely related bacteria
questions.stem: A ventilated ICU patient has pneumonia. Gram stain of a respiratory sample shows the organisms indicated, which are between rods and spheres in shape. The isolate is non-motile, oxidase-negative, forms colorless colonies, and is resistant to carbapenems. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Acinetobacter spp. are gram-negative coccobacilli that are non-motile and oxidase-negative, with colorless or creamy colonies. A. baumannii is a leading cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia and often shows multidrug resistance, including carbapenem resistance. Pseudomonas is a motile, oxidase-positive, pigmented bacillus.
